title: Jeremiah 51:45–58
context: The LORD calls his people a third time to leave Babylon (51:45; compare 50:8 and 51:6) and not to lose heart at rumors (51:46). He promises judgment on Babylon’s images, the joy of heaven and earth (51:47–48), and a call to the escaped to remember Jerusalem (51:50). The people lament the defilement of the sanctuary (51:51), and the LORD answers that Babylon’s walls and gates will fall (51:52–58). The poem’s images of total devastation differ from the commonly reported account of Babylon’s capture by Persia in 539 BC without large-scale destruction; the difference is noted, not resolved.

verses.text: “My people, go away from the middle of her, and each of you save yourselves from the LORD’s fierce anger.
verses.arminianNotes: “My people, go away from the middle of her, and each of you save yourselves from the LORD’s fierce anger.” Arminian readers see the third call to flee Babylon.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the call to depart before judgment. Readers in this tradition see the repeated summons (50:8; 51:6) as shared ground on God’s care to rescue his people from a doomed city.

verses.text: Don’t let your heart faint. Don’t fear for the news that will be heard in the land. For news will come one year, and after that in another year news will come, and violence in the land, ruler against ruler.
verses.arminianNotes: “Don’t let your heart faint. Don’t fear for the news that will be heard in the land.” Arminian readers see God encouraging his people through rumors and turmoil.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see pastoral comfort amid uncertainty. Readers in this tradition note that the LORD prepares his people for confusing times so that they will not lose heart.

verses.text: Therefore behold, the days come that I will execute judgment on the engraved images of Babylon; and her whole land will be confounded. All her slain will fall in the middle of her.
verses.arminianNotes: “Therefore behold, the days come that I will execute judgment on the engraved images of Babylon.” Arminian readers see judgment on Babylon’s idols as central to its fall.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD judging false gods. Readers in this tradition note the repeated focus on idols in these chapters, showing that the conflict is ultimately between the LORD and Babylon’s gods.

verses.text: Then the heavens and the earth, and all that is therein, will sing for joy over Babylon; for the destroyers will come to her from the north,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: “Then the heavens and the earth, and all that is therein, will sing for joy over Babylon.” Arminian readers see creation rejoicing at the fall of oppression.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see cosmic joy at God’s justice. Revelation 18:20 calls heaven to rejoice over Babylon’s fall, cited here by reference; readers in this tradition hold the echo as a later reuse.

verses.text: “As Babylon has caused the slain of Israel to fall, so the slain of all the land will fall at Babylon.
verses.arminianNotes: “As Babylon has caused the slain of Israel to fall, so the slain of all the land will fall at Babylon.” Arminian readers see measure-for-measure justice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see recompense matching Babylon’s deeds. Readers in this tradition read the verse soberly, as a statement of justice rather than an invitation to delight in suffering.

verses.text: You who have escaped the sword, go! Don’t stand still! Remember the LORD from afar, and let Jerusalem come into your mind.”
verses.arminianNotes: “You who have escaped the sword, go! Don’t stand still! Remember the LORD from afar, and let Jerusalem come into your mind.” Arminian readers see exiles called to remember God and Zion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the call to leave and to remember the LORD. Readers in this tradition see memory of Jerusalem as an act of faith that keeps the exiles oriented toward God’s promises.

verses.text: “We are confounded because we have heard reproach. Confusion has covered our faces, for strangers have come into the sanctuaries of the LORD’s house.”
verses.arminianNotes: The people answer, “We are confounded because we have heard reproach.” Arminian readers hear grief that strangers have entered the sanctuary of the LORD’s house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the people’s shame over the temple’s defilement. Readers in this tradition note that the LORD answers this lament in the next verse with a promise of judgment on Babylon.

verses.text: “Therefore behold, the days come,” says the LORD, “that I will execute judgment on her engraved images; and through all her land the wounded will groan.
verses.arminianNotes: “Therefore behold, the days come,” says the LORD, “that I will execute judgment on her engraved images.” Arminian readers see God answering his people’s shame with judgment on Babylon’s idols.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD responding to the lament of 51:51. Readers in this tradition note the repetition of 51:47, reinforcing the certainty of judgment on false gods.

verses.text: Though Babylon should mount up to the sky, and though she should fortify the height of her strength, yet destroyers will come to her from me,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: “Though Babylon should mount up to the sky … yet destroyers will come to her from me,” says the LORD. Arminian readers see that no height of human pride can escape God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the futility of Babylon’s fortifications. Some readers hear an echo of Babel’s tower in Genesis 11:4, though readers in this tradition hold that connection as suggestive.

verses.text: “The sound of a cry comes from Babylon, and of great destruction from the land of the Chaldeans!
verses.arminianNotes: “The sound of a cry comes from Babylon, and of great destruction from the land of the Chaldeans!” Arminian readers see the cry of judgment rising from the city.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the cry signaling Babylon’s fall. Readers in this tradition note that the cry of the oppressed is now heard from the oppressor, a reversal of fortunes.

verses.text: For the LORD lays Babylon waste, and destroys out of her the great voice! Their waves roar like many waters. The noise of their voice is uttered.
verses.arminianNotes: “For the LORD lays Babylon waste, and destroys out of her the great voice!” Arminian readers see the silencing of Babylon’s proud noise by the LORD’s judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD silencing Babylon. The roaring waves of the attackers replace Babylon’s great voice, and readers in this tradition see God’s sovereignty over the clamor of nations.

verses.text: For the destroyer has come on her, even on Babylon. Her mighty men are taken. Their bows are broken in pieces, for the LORD is a God of retribution. He will surely repay.
verses.arminianNotes: “… the LORD is a God of retribution. He will surely repay.” Arminian readers see God’s justice as certain, repaying Babylon for its deeds.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise affirm the LORD as a God of retribution. Readers in both traditions commonly see shared ground here: God’s justice is sure, and his people may leave vengeance to him.

verses.text: I will make her princes, her wise men, her governors, her deputies, and her mighty men drunk. They will sleep a perpetual sleep, and not wake up,” says the King, whose name is the LORD of Armies.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will make her princes, her wise men … drunk. They will sleep a perpetual sleep,” says the King, whose name is the LORD of Armies. Arminian readers see Babylon’s leaders brought to an end.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see judgment on Babylon’s leaders. The title “the King” sets the LORD above Babylon’s king, and readers in this tradition see in it the sovereignty that governs the whole oracle.

verses.text: The LORD of Armies says: “The wide walls of Babylon will be utterly overthrown. Her high gates will be burned with fire. The peoples will labor for vanity, and the nations for the fire; and they will be weary.”
verses.arminianNotes: “The wide walls of Babylon will be utterly overthrown.” Arminian readers see the end of Babylon’s fortifications and the futility of labor spent on what God will judge.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the vanity of human building apart from God. The line “The peoples will labor for vanity” resembles Habakkuk 2:13, cited by reference, and readers in this tradition note the similar wording.
